questions.question: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL in SQL?
questions.title: UNION vs UNION ALL in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **UNION** combines results of two queries and removes duplicates (adds a DISTINCT step). **UNION ALL** combines results and keeps all rows including duplicates. UNION ALL is faster because it skips the deduplication step.

interviewer_intent.testing: UNION vs UNION ALL semantics and performance
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using UNION when UNION ALL would work and be faster
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that UNION requires same number and compatible types of columns from both queries

rows: Know data is distinct OR want all rows

sections.title: UNION vs UNION ALL Example
sections.content:
-- UNION: removes duplicates between result sets
SELECT name FROM employees_us
UNION
SELECT name FROM employees_uk;

-- UNION ALL: keeps all rows including duplicates
SELECT name FROM employees_us
UNION ALL
SELECT name FROM employees_uk;

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: UNION and UNION ALL both combine the results of two SELECT queries, but they differ in duplicate handling. UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result — it performs an implicit DISTINCT. UNION ALL keeps all rows, including duplicates from both queries. The performance implication is that UNION must sort and compare all rows to remove duplicates, making it slower. If you know the two queries will not produce duplicate rows, or if you want all rows, use UNION ALL. Both require the same number of columns in each SELECT and compatible data types.

questions.question: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP in SQL?
questions.title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **DELETE** (DML) removes specific rows, can be rolled back, fires triggers. **TRUNCATE** (DDL) removes all rows instantly, resets auto-increment, cannot be rolled back. **DROP** (DDL) permanently removes the entire table and its structure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical differences between data removal commands
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using DELETE to clear a large table when TRUNCATE would be 100x faster
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that TRUNCATE resets auto-increment counter and why that matters for data integrity

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP all remove data but in very different ways. DELETE is DML — it removes rows matching a WHERE clause and can be rolled back. Each deletion is logged, so it is slower for large amounts of data. TRUNCATE is DDL — it removes all rows at once by deallocating data pages, cannot be rolled back, resets the auto-increment counter, and is much faster. DROP removes the entire table including its structure and indexes, also cannot be rolled back. Use DELETE for selective removal, TRUNCATE to quickly clear all data while keeping the table, and DROP when you want the table completely gone.

followup_questions: Why is TRUNCATE faster than DELETE?
What happens to the auto-increment counter after TRUNCATE?
Can you use WHERE with TRUNCATE?

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
questions.title: WHERE vs HAVING in SQL — Row vs Group Filtering
questions.direct_answer: **WHERE** filters individual rows before GROUP BY. **HAVING** filters groups after GROUP BY. WHERE cannot use aggregate functions; HAVING can. For performance, use WHERE to reduce rows before the expensive grouping step.

interviewer_intent.testing: WHERE vs HAVING execution order and use cases
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using HAVING for non-aggregate conditions that should be in WHERE
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a combined WHERE + HAVING query and explain each clause's role

sections.title: WHERE + HAVING Combined
sections.content:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 40000
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: WHERE and HAVING are both filters but they operate at different stages. WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping — it cannot use aggregate functions because they have not been computed yet. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregate functions. A practical example: to find departments where more than 3 employees earn above 40000, put the salary condition in WHERE to filter rows first, then put the COUNT condition in HAVING to filter the resulting groups. This is more efficient than putting both in HAVING.

questions.question: What is the difference between JOIN and a subquery in SQL?
questions.title: JOIN vs Subquery in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **JOINs** combine rows from multiple tables and can return columns from both. **Subqueries** are nested queries used for filtering or computing values. JOINs are usually more performant; subqueries can be more readable for complex filtering.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical ability to choose between JOIN and subquery
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using correlated subqueries where a JOIN would be significantly faster
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the same query written both ways and explain optimizer behavior

sections.title: JOIN vs Subquery
sections.content:
-- Subquery approach
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE amount > 500);

-- JOIN approach (often faster)
SELECT DISTINCT c.name
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.amount > 500;

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: JOINs and subqueries serve different purposes. JOINs combine rows from multiple tables and let you select columns from all joined tables. Subqueries are nested queries used for filtering, existence checks, or computing scalar values. JOINs are generally more performant because the query optimizer has more flexibility in executing join operations. Correlated subqueries that run once per outer row can be very slow. However, subqueries can be more readable for complex filtering logic. Modern optimizers often rewrite subqueries as joins internally, so the performance difference may be minimal in simple cases.

questions.question: What is the difference between CHAR and VARCHAR in SQL?
questions.title: CHAR vs VARCHAR in SQL — Fixed vs Variable Length
questions.direct_answer: **CHAR(n)** is fixed-length — always stores exactly n characters, padding with spaces. **VARCHAR(n)** is variable-length — stores only the actual characters plus 1-2 bytes for length. CHAR is faster for fixed-length data (like country codes); VARCHAR saves space for variable-length data.

interviewer_intent.testing: String data type choice and storage implications
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using CHAR for long variable-length strings and wasting space
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that CHAR trailing spaces are stripped on retrieval in MySQL, and when CHAR is actually faster

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: CHAR and VARCHAR are both string types but they store data differently. CHAR is fixed length — CHAR of 10 always occupies 10 bytes, padding shorter strings with spaces. VARCHAR is variable length — it only uses as much space as the actual string plus 1 or 2 bytes to store the length. CHAR is slightly faster for retrieval because rows have fixed-length fields at known offsets. VARCHAR saves storage for variable-length data. Use CHAR for values that are always the same length — like two-letter country codes or phone numbers with fixed format — and VARCHAR for names, emails, and other variable-length data.

questions.question: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and WHERE in a multi-table query?
questions.title: INNER JOIN vs WHERE for Multi-Table Queries
questions.direct_answer: Using `FROM a, b WHERE a.id = b.a_id` (old-style) and `FROM a INNER JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id` produce the same result. Modern ANSI JOIN syntax is preferred for readability, explicit intent, and because it separates join conditions from filter conditions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of old vs new JOIN syntax
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that old FROM a, b syntax is a cross join if WHERE condition is omitted
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that modern JOIN syntax is preferred because it clearly separates join logic from filter logic

sections.title: Old Style vs ANSI JOIN Syntax
sections.content:
-- Old style (implicit join): works but avoid
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name
FROM employees e, departments d
WHERE e.dept_id = d.id AND e.salary > 50000;

-- ANSI JOIN syntax (preferred)
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
WHERE e.salary > 50000;

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Old style (FROM a, b WHERE a.id = b.id): implicit cross join with filter in WHERE
- ANSI JOIN syntax: explicit, separates join condition (ON) from filter (WHERE)
- If WHERE condition is accidentally omitted in old style: full CROSS JOIN
- ANSI syntax makes outer joins much clearer (LEFT JOIN vs WHERE tricks)
- Modern codebases and code reviews prefer ANSI JOIN syntax
- Same performance when equivalently written

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The old-style multi-table query with FROM employees, departments WHERE employees.dept_id equals departments.id is an implicit join — it is technically a cross join filtered by a WHERE condition. The modern ANSI JOIN syntax with INNER JOIN and ON achieves the same result but is preferred because it makes the intent explicit and separates join conditions from filter conditions. The practical danger of the old style is that forgetting the WHERE condition accidentally creates a full cross join returning millions of rows. ANSI syntax eliminates this ambiguity, and makes outer joins much more readable.
